title: What JdbcTemplate does around your SQL
summary: Take a connection, run the statement, map the rows, translate any failure, release the connection. The interesting parts are the first and last: where the connection comes from, and what happens to a SQLException.
entry: Put a breakpoint in DataSourceUtils.doGetConnection and run one query with a transaction and once without. The branch you land on is the whole lesson.

steps.notice: The template method every other operation funnels into. query, update and batchUpdate are all thin wrappers that supply a callback; read this one and you have read them all.

The branch that matters. If a transaction has bound a connection to this thread it is reused; otherwise a fresh one is taken from the pool. This is why two statements outside a transaction use two connections and two inside it use one.
The mirror image: a connection belonging to a transaction is left alone, and only a standalone one is actually closed. Getting this wrong by hand is how connection leaks happen.
Where the default translator is chosen. Since Framework 6 it is SQLExceptionSubclassTranslator unless you supply an error-codes file, in which case the old vendor-code translator is used instead.
Maps JDBC 4 SQLException subclasses onto Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy. Short and worth reading, because it is what makes a duplicate key mean the same thing on every database.
The chain: custom translator, then the specific one, then the fallback. Nothing ever escapes as a checked SQLException, which is why no Spring data access method declares throws.
The Framework 6.1 facade. It delegates to JdbcTemplate or NamedParameterJdbcTemplate depending on which param() overload you use, and adds optional() so a missing row is not an exception.
